newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW -- US April retail sales slip 0.3 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- US April retail sales slip 0.3 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department said retail sales fell 0.3 percent in April. Excluding the hefty automobile component, sales fell 0.1 percent.
Economists had expected sales to fall 0.3 percent overall and rise 0.1 percent minus cars.
JOHN LONSKI, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MOODY'S INVESTORS SERVICE: "This (report) raises prospects for monetary policy being left unchanged on May 20.

ANTHONY CHAN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANC ONE INVESTMENT: "Certainly the ex-autos number is a little bit on the weaker side, indicating things are a bit weaker than expected. The department chain store sales number came in slightly weaker than expected, again suggesting a pause in activity.
"I think a lot of it was due to the weather being cooler, discouraging a lot of people from buying spring clothing.

"The numbers still don't show a distinct slowing unless we see this happening for a few more months. The numbers will be very encouraging to the market. The (money) market was expecting these numbers to be a bit on the stronger side."

JAMES PADINHA, ECONOMIST, BRIEFING.COM: "It probably just confirms the perceptions that people had about April as a spending month...kind of a hangover, if you will, after a really strong first quarter.
"As far as Fed implications, I can't imagine that this would sway the Fed too much. We still know little about the pace of demand going forward.

"So all in all what the market expected although the (Treasury) market is up. People want to see weak final demand numbers and low inflation....the first part of that equation is satisfied and maybe Thursday we'll get the second part."

MICHAEL STRAUSS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, SANWA SECURITIES (USA) CO: "Some of the good news was built in, but not all of it. The market will probably get excited about the fact that for the last two months, retail sales were basically flat. That obviously discounts some of the ... surge in spending we had in January and February.

"The debate now will begin about what was the culprit for the spending pattern we had, January and February being a boom and March and April being a bust. The surge in January and February depleted inventories in March and April.
"This may be a number that keeps the Fed on the sidelines next week."

GARY THAYER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, AG EDWARDS & SONS INC: "Good numbers for the economy. Hold up at relatively decent levels but not so strong as to force (the Federal Reserve) to raise rates in the near future.
"We've seen weak retail sales, department store sales look soft -- so this suggests the economy may be slowing down to a more sustainable rate of growth in the second quarter."
